claims.text: Effective communication is the transfer of a message from a sender to a receiver such that the receiver understands it as the sender intended and can act on it; a message that is sent but never understood has not communicated anything.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Internal communication is the exchange of messages between people inside a business - managers, employees and departments; external communication is the exchange between the business and outside parties such as customers, suppliers, lenders, government and the local community.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Effective communication tends to reduce errors, wasted time and misunderstanding inside a business and supports motivation, because people who understand what to do and why usually work more accurately and with more commitment; ineffective communication tends to produce rework, accidents, missed orders and lost sales.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Communication is a two-way process: feedback from the receiver - a reply, a question or an observable action - is what tells the sender whether the message was understood.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The methods a business can use to communicate fall into spoken (face-to-face conversation, meetings, telephone and video calls), written on paper (notices, letters, memos, reports), visual (diagrams, signs, plans) and IT-based (email, instant messaging, intranets, websites and social media pages).

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: IT-based methods tend to be fast and cheap once equipment and connectivity are in place, reach many receivers at once and leave a timestamped record; they depend on electricity, networks and the receiver actually reading the message, and they carry security risks such as interception or impersonation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Spoken methods allow immediate feedback and carry tone and body language, which suits complex or sensitive messages, but they leave no record unless written down and can be slow and costly when many people must take part; paper-written methods leave a permanent record but travel slowly and cannot be questioned.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: No single method suits every message: the right choice depends on the audience's access and habits, the urgency of the message, the need for a record or for immediate feedback, the sensitivity of the content and the cost per receiver.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Recommending a communication method means matching the features of the candidate methods to the stated circumstances - audience, urgency, record, feedback, sensitivity and cost - rather than naming the method with the most benefits in general.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A justified recommendation states the choice, weighs the decisive criterion against the strongest alternative, and names the condition under which the choice holds, such as the audience actually using the channel.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A communication barrier is anything that prevents a message from reaching its receiver or distorts it so that it is not understood as intended; the objectives of a communication - informing, instructing, persuading - are the results it is meant to achieve, and a barrier is an obstacle standing in the way of those results.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Barriers tend to arise from the sender's choices or the setting: jargon the receiver has not learned, information overload, the wrong channel for the audience, background noise, differences of language, and messages that pass through many hands and distort at each step.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Ineffective communication tends to cost a business in errors, rework, wasted time, missed orders and damaged customer relationships, and it can lower motivation among staff who feel unheard.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Barriers can be reduced or removed by choosing a channel the audience uses, writing in plain language, keeping messages short and ordered, inviting feedback that confirms understanding, and training staff in the channels the business relies on.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
